docs.title: AI access (MCP server)
docs.text:
Pierside can let an AI assistant such as Claude Code work with your Docker engines, with limits you set: from reading the logs of one project up to nearly everything Pierside's own window can do. It does this through a built-in MCP server: the assistant gets a fixed set of tools, never Docker itself, and Pierside checks every call against the permissions of the connection it came from.

Nothing is shared until you create a connection.

docs.title: Create a connection
docs.text:
1. Open AI access at the bottom of the sidebar and choose New connection.
  2. Give it a name and choose which engines it may use: the local one, SSH engines, or all of them. The first one ticked is the default; the assistant can list the engines and name another one in each call.
  3. Choose which containers it covers: all of them, or tick them in the list. Ticking a Compose project covers its containers, including ones it gets later. Below the list you can add name patterns for containers or projects that don't exist yet: * matches any text, so shop-* covers shop-web and shop-db.
  4. Tick what the assistant may do (see below).
  5. Choose how the assistant gets in (see the next section) and create it.
  6. In the dialog that opens, choose Add to Claude Code or Add to Devin CLI. The dialog shows the command the button runs; where there is no button (see below), run that command in a terminal yourself.

The Add to … button runs the command shown in the dialog for you (claude mcp add … or devin mcp add …) and replaces an older entry of the same name. With Available in all my projects switched off, choose the project folder first: the command then runs in that folder and the assistant has the access only there. The entry stays in your own assistant settings; nothing is written into the folder. It appears when Pierside runs inside Rancher Desktop and finds the assistant installed for your user; a running Claude Code session picks the new server up with /mcp or at its next start. Removing a connection in Pierside also removes it from the assistants that have it under that name.

For Claude Code the command looks like this:

claude mcp add --scope user pierside-webshop -- docker exec -i <pierside container> python -m app.mcp_stdio --profile 1a2b3c4d5e6f

With --scope user Claude Code has the access in all your projects. Without Available in all my projects the command has no such flag and registers the access only for the project folder it is run in. In Claude Code, /mcp shows whether it is connected.

The dialog's Devin CLI tab has the same command for Devin's command-line tool:

devin mcp add -s user pierside-webshop -- docker exec -i <pierside container> python -m app.mcp_stdio --profile 1a2b3c4d5e6f

-s user plays the role of --scope user; without it Devin registers the access only for the project folder you run it in. devin mcp list shows the servers it knows.

The last tab has the same thing as JSON for other MCP clients.

docs.title: You allow it in Pierside (the default)
docs.text:
The command contains no secret. The first time the assistant uses a tool, Pierside shows a question with a four-letter code. That first tool call comes back after a few seconds so that the assistant can tell you the same code in its reply; compare the two, then answer:

  • Allow this session: until that assistant session ends. The next session asks again.
  • Allow longer: for 24 hours, 7 days, 30 days, or always. During that time no question is asked.
  • Deny.

After you allow it, the assistant calls the tool again. The question stays open in Pierside for ten minutes, so a late answer still counts.

You can also set the trust period in the connection's settings, and withdraw it at any time with stop trusting on the AI access page. Sessions that are running are then asked again.

If the connection may change things, Pierside can also ask before each such action and shows exactly what the assistant is about to do. Ask before each action in the connection's settings has three choices:

  • Every action that changes something (the default),
  • Only deleting, overwriting and running commands (starting a container with a folder of the host mounted counts as this too, since it can change files on your machine),
  • Never.

"Always trust" together with "Never" means the assistant is not held up by any question.

Keep in mind what trust means: while a connection is trusted, any program on your computer that can run Docker can use it without asking. That program could already do more with Docker directly, so this is a convenience trade-off, not a new hole.

docs.title: Access token
docs.text: For assistants that run unattended and can't wait for a click. The command then carries a token (-e PIERSIDE_MCP_TOKEN=pmcp_…), shown only once; Pierside stores only a hash of it. It works without asking you, until you make a new token with the key button or remove the connection. Don't commit a configuration file that contains it.

docs.title: Permissions
docs.text: The assistant is only offered the tools you allowed. It can always list the engines of the connection, the shared containers and their Compose projects, and it can ask what the connection allows (its permissions, file paths and limits), so it doesn't have to find out by trial and error.

docs.title: Shared containers
docs.text:
These apply to the containers chosen under Which containers.

Permission What the assistant can do Read logs Recent log lines of a container or a whole Compose project, filtered by text, by the last N minutes, or by a time window in the past. See the limits below. See configuration and state Image, command, ports, networks, mounts, labels, restart policy; live CPU and memory use, running processes, health check results, files changed since start, the equivalent docker run command. Environment variables show only their names unless you tick the option to show values. Start, stop, restart Also pause, resume and kill; single containers and whole Compose projects Create, rename, delete Run a new container from an image (name, ports, environment, volumes, restart policy, network); recreate a container with the same settings, for example to pick up a newer image; rename and delete containers Compose up and down Read a project's Compose files and its resolved configuration, bring the project up (also after a change, or when it is down) and take it down. SSH engines only, see below. Run commands Any shell command inside the containers, optionally as a given user and in a given folder, with a time limit of up to two minutes. A command that runs past its limit is reported as an error but is not stopped.

Log limits. A request returns the newest 200 lines unless the assistant asks for more, and never more than the connection's Most log lines per request (500 unless you change it, at most 5000). A text filter searches only that many newest lines of the requested time window, not the whole log. "Allow everything" connections use the maximum, 5000. Any single answer is also cut at 200,000 characters.

A new or renamed container must have a name the connection covers. New containers can't mount the Docker socket, system folders of the host such as /etc, /usr or /var/lib/docker (or a folder that contains one, such as /var), or the volumes of Pierside and other extensions. A host path with a symbolic link in it is refused too, and so is a path inside a folder that a container the assistant can reach mounts writable: otherwise the assistant could make a link there that leads to a system folder. Mounting a volume that already exists also needs See volumes. They can't use the host's network or share another container's (container:…). They can join any network the connection may see, including a macvlan or ipvlan network if the engine has one: that puts the container on your local network (not into the host's own).

Allow mounting host system folders lifts the mount rule. It appears only under Allow everything and is off unless you switch it on. With it, the assistant can start a container with the Docker socket or /var/lib/docker mounted, which is full control of the engine's machine: it reaches everything that is otherwise kept back, including Pierside's own data with your saved SSH keys and passwords. Use it only on an engine where that is acceptable.

docs.title: Files
docs.text:
Permission What the assistant can do Read files List folders, read text files up to 1 MB, and search file contents, only under the paths you list Change files Write or replace text files up to 1 MB, create folders, delete, change permissions, under the same paths

List one path pattern per line. * matches within one folder, ** also across folders:

  • /etc/nginx/** allows everything under /etc/nginx
  • /app/config/*.yaml allows the YAML files directly in /app/config

Nothing is reachable until you add a path. A path that goes through a symbolic link is refused, so a link inside an allowed folder can't be used to reach something outside it. A search looks only into files the patterns allow, also below the folder it starts in; it stops after 30 seconds and never reads /proc, /sys or /dev.

docs.title: The whole engine
docs.text:
These are not limited to the shared containers.

Permission What the assistant can do See images List images, their details and layers Pull images Download an image to the engine See volumes List volumes and their details. Reading files in a volume also needs Read files, and its paths apply inside the volume. See networks List networks and what is attached Connect networks Connect a shared container to a network, or disconnect it See ports Published and exposed ports of the shared containers, and Pierside's port forwards Forward ports Make a shared container's port reachable at localhost on your computer, and remove such forwards Engine info Docker version, CPUs and memory, disk usage, and recent engine events such as crashes and out-of-memory kills See Swarm Nodes, stacks, services and their tasks, service logs, and the names (never the contents) of secrets and configs Change Swarm services Create, scale, restart, change the image, roll back and remove services; remove a stack. Deploying a stack from a Compose file is not available. Create volumes and networks New named volumes and networks Delete and clean up Delete images, volumes and networks, and prune what is unused: stopped shared containers, images, volumes, networks, build cache. A preview shows what a prune would delete without deleting anything.

docs.title: Allow everything
docs.text: One switch at the top of the dialog: every container, every permission above, all file paths, and environment values visible, on the engines you choose under Which engines. Pick a single engine there to give full access to that one only, or All engines. The connection is marked in red on the AI access page. How the assistant gets in, and whether it asks before each action, are still your choice.

docs.title: Compose on the local engine
docs.text: Compose up, down and reading Compose files work on SSH engines, where Pierside runs docker compose on the server. On the local engine Compose runs through Rancher Desktop's window, which a connection can't use. There the assistant can start, stop and restart a project's existing containers and recreate single containers, and it is told where the Compose files are on your computer so it can read them from disk itself.

docs.title: Asking for more
docs.text:
When the assistant needs something its connection doesn't allow, it can ask you instead of stopping. Pierside shows what it asks for (a permission, a container or Compose project, a file path, an engine, or the values of environment variables) with the assistant's reason, and you answer:

  • Allow this session: that assistant session has it until it ends; the connection itself doesn't change.
  • Add to connection: it becomes part of the connection, as if you had ticked it in the dialog.
  • Deny: refused; the assistant may ask for something else.
  • Deny, pause 2 min: refused, and that assistant session can't ask for more access for two minutes.

Decide by the list of what would be allowed. The reason is written by the assistant, and text in a log or a file can talk an assistant into asking. The request waits in Pierside for ten minutes.

The assistant can't ask for Allow everything, for mounting host system folders, or to change how it is trusted or when it is asked; those you set yourself. Asking is available for connections you allow in Pierside, not for access tokens, and you can switch it off per connection with The assistant may ask for more access.

docs.title: What the assistant can't do
docs.text:
• Add or remove engines.
  • Run commands on a server itself, outside containers. (Compose on an SSH engine is the one exception, and only for the projects the connection covers.)
  • Read the contents of Swarm secrets.

docs.title: What is never shared
docs.text:
Not even with "Allow everything":

  • Containers, volumes and networks that belong to Pierside itself, to other Rancher Desktop extensions, or to Kubernetes. Pierside's container holds the Docker socket and your saved SSH credentials.
  • Containers a connection doesn't cover. To the assistant they look the same as containers that don't exist.

docs.title: Things to keep in mind
docs.text:
• Logs and files can contain secrets. Passwords printed at start-up, tokens in config files and the values of environment variables go to the assistant, and so to the AI provider, if you allow them. Share narrowly.
  • Image details can contain secrets too. With environment values hidden, the build history still shows RUN lines as they were written; a secret typed directly into a Dockerfile command is visible there.
  • Run commands removes the other limits for the containers it covers: a command can read any file and change anything inside them. Leave it off unless you need it.
  • The engine-wide permissions show more than the shared containers. See images and See networks list everything of that kind on the engine. See volumes lists the volumes that are unused or used only by shared containers (all volumes when the connection shares all containers): a volume holds the data of the containers using it. Lists of a network's or volume's containers name only shared ones. Engine info gives totals for the whole engine, but names only what the connection can see anyway: its own containers in engine events and in the largest items of disk usage, and images, volumes and networks only with the permission for them.
  • Container output is untrusted text. A container can print something that reads like instructions. Read-only connections limit what such text could cause.
  • A connection that uses an access token keeps that token in the assistant's configuration in plain text. Prefer the approval mode unless the assistant must run unattended.

docs.title: Manage connections
docs.text:
On the AI access page each connection has:

  • a switch to turn it off and on without removing it,
  • a button that shows the connection command again (or, for token connections, a key button that creates a new token and makes the old one stop working at once),
  • how it is trusted right now, with stop trusting where that applies,
  • edit and remove.

Changes apply to the next call; the assistant doesn't need to reconnect, except after a new token. When a change adds or removes tools, Pierside tells the assistant that its tool list changed (within half a minute); Claude Code then reloads it by itself.

Recent activity lists the latest calls: which connection, which tool, which container or file, and whether it was allowed. Refused calls, including ones you denied or didn't answer, are marked. The list is kept in memory and starts empty when Pierside restarts.

docs.title: Requirements and limits
docs.text:
• The assistant reaches Pierside through docker exec, so it needs the docker command on your computer, and Rancher Desktop and Pierside must be running.
  • The connection keeps working when Pierside is updated. It stops if you install Pierside from a different image name (for example a build of your own), because the container name in the command changes; copy the command again with the key button.
  • Connections are stored in Pierside's data volume and survive updates.

docs.title: Alerts and notifications
docs.text:
While Pierside is open it watches the active engine and tells you about problems you would otherwise only find by looking:

Problem When Pierside reports it Out of memory A container was killed by the system for using more memory than it may. Unhealthy A container's health check started failing. Keeps restarting A container exited by itself three times within five minutes and Docker started it again each time. Swarm task keeps failing The same task of a Swarm service failed three times within five minutes, on any node.

Each one appears as a message at the bottom right of the window.

docs.title: How often
docs.text:
Pierside tells you about a problem once, not about every failure:

  • While it goes on, it stays quiet. A container that was reported isn't reported again, for any reason, while it keeps failing: a container in a restart loop also turns unhealthy after each start, and that isn't a second alert. A Swarm service is one alert, however many of its tasks fail.
  • A reminder every two hours if it never stops, saying how long it has been going on.
  • After fifteen minutes without a failure the problem is over. If it starts again after that, it is reported again.
  • Alerts arriving together are one message ("3 alerts"), not a queue of messages one after another. The message stays while the pointer is on it.

In the message:

  • Mute 1 h silences what the message is about (that container, by its name, so also when it is recreated; that Swarm service; that engine) for an hour. Mute these 1 h does that for every alert in a message with several.
  • Pause all 15 min silences every alert for a quarter of an hour, for example while you are fixing the problem.

Both also silence the desktop notifications, and last when you switch engines.

docs.title: Restart loops
docs.text:
A container is in a restart loop when it has a restart policy (always, unless-stopped, on-failure) and keeps exiting. Pierside tells two kinds apart, because the fix differs:

  • It keeps crashing (exit code other than 0): something is wrong in the container. The message gives the exit code; look at its logs.
  • Its command keeps finishing (exit code 0): the container does its job, ends, and Docker starts it again. If it is meant to run once, change its restart policy to no or on-failure.

Stopping, restarting or killing a container yourself is never counted, whether you do it in Pierside, with docker, or with Compose: Docker marks those differently from a container that exits by itself. Docker waits longer before each new attempt, up to a minute, which is why the window is five minutes.

A container without such a restart policy is never reported, however often it exits: Docker doesn't restart it, so something else is starting it again. CI runners do this, for example GitLab Runner reuses its job containers for each stage of a job.

On the Containers page, a container that is restarting or unhealthy also shows in the sidebar's red badge.

docs.title: Swarm services
docs.text: A failing Swarm task is replaced by a new one each time, possibly on another node, so Pierside looks at the service's tasks instead of at single containers, twice a minute. It reports a service when the same task slot (for a global service: the same node) failed or was rejected three times within five minutes, and gives Swarm's reason, for example a non-zero exit code or an image that can't be found. Several replicas of a service each finishing once is not reported. When several of a service's tasks keep failing, as with an image that doesn't exist, it is one alert for the service. The same Swarm added as more than one engine (several managers) is reported once. This needs the active engine to be a Swarm manager.

docs.title: Server alerts
docs.text:
For an SSH engine, switch on Alert me about this server on its Server performance page. Pierside then checks that server every 30 seconds, whichever engine is active, and tells you when:

  • memory is almost full (less than 10 % available, on two checks in a row);
  • it keeps swapping (more than 1 MB/s on two checks in a row): memory is short, and everything slows down;
  • the load stays high (more than 1.5 per CPU over 5 minutes, on three checks in a row);
  • a disk is almost full (90 %, and as an error from 97 %).

A short spike isn't reported. The same alert comes again after half an hour at the earliest, a full disk after six hours.

docs.title: Desktop notifications
docs.text:
Click the version number in the bottom bar and switch on Desktop notifications for container problems. Pierside then also shows a notification of your operating system for each alert, at most one every 30 seconds: alerts in between come together in the next one. Switching it on shows a sample, so you can see that it works on your computer.

  • In Rancher Desktop the notification is shown by Rancher Desktop itself. Its title is always "Warning" or "Error"; the text starts with "Pierside" and says what happened and on which engine. Clicking it does nothing. It appears for every alert, also while you are looking at Pierside.
  • In the separate window it is your browser's notification, which asks for permission once. Clicking it goes to the container's logs or the service. It appears only when the Pierside window isn't the one in front.

With Pierside open in Rancher Desktop and in the separate window at the same time, each shows its own notification, so you get two.

Alerts cover the engine that is active, and every engine you watch in the background (Engines at a glance, see Remote engines); an alert about another engine than the active one starts with its name. A watched engine that can't be reached is reported too, and again when it is back.

Notifications need Pierside to be open: in Rancher Desktop with the Pierside tab shown, or in the separate window. Watched engines are watched while Rancher Desktop runs, even with Pierside closed; what happened in the meantime is listed under Recent alerts on the Engines at a glance page (until Rancher Desktop is restarted). The active engine is watched only while Pierside is open, unless you watch it in the background too.

docs.title: Building from source
docs.text: You need Rancher Desktop (dockerd engine). The image build needs nothing else; Node.js 22 is only needed for the UI dev server.

docs.title: Build and install
docs.text:
docker build -t pierside/extension:dev .
rdctl extension install pierside/extension:dev

Or with the helper scripts (make on Linux/macOS, make.ps1 in PowerShell):

./make.ps1 build       # docker build -t pierside/extension:dev .
./make.ps1 install     # build + install
./make.ps1 reinstall   # build + uninstall + install
./make.ps1 logs        # follow the backend's logs
./make.ps1 dev         # UI dev server on http://localhost:3000

Use reinstall after changes: installing a tag that is already installed does nothing in Rancher Desktop.

To bake in a version number: docker build --build-arg VERSION=1.2.3 -t … .

docs.title: How it is put together
docs.text:
• UI (ui/): React, TypeScript, Vite, MUI. Rancher Desktop loads it as the extension's tab.
  • Backend (backend/): Python 3.12, FastAPI, aiodocker. It runs as the extension's container with the Docker socket mounted and serves the UI's requests, plus WebSockets for logs, stats, events and shells on a localhost port.
  • Packaging: Dockerfile builds the UI, then assembles the image with the backend, metadata.json and docker-compose.yaml.

docs.title: UI dev server
docs.text:
1. Install the extension once; its backend keeps running.
  2. ./make.ps1 dev (or make dev) finds the backend's port and starts Vite.
  3. Open http://localhost:3000/#/containers in a browser.

The UI then talks to the installed backend directly. Features that need Rancher Desktop itself (local Compose, the Docker console) are unavailable there.

docs.title: Changelog
docs.text: Each release of Pierside, newest first. Install a specific one with rdctl extension install ghcr.io/hemi131/pierside:<version>.

• Website: Pierside has its own site, pierside.dev, with an overview of what it does, the installation guide, the documentation (with search) and this changelog. Pierside's About dialog (click the version in the footer) links to it.

• Terminals: Ctrl+S no longer freezes the shell. It used to stop all output until Ctrl+Q (the terminal's old flow control), which looked like a hung shell. Full-screen programs such as nano still get it.
  • Terminals (the server terminal of an SSH engine and a container's shell): right click works as in Windows Terminal: it copies the selected text, or pastes when nothing is selected.
  • The server terminal of an SSH engine edits the command line by word, as a container's shell already did: Ctrl+Backspace and Ctrl+Delete delete a word, Ctrl+Left / Ctrl+Right move by word, and text is selected with Shift+arrows, by word with Ctrl+Shift+Left / Right, or to the line's ends with Shift+Home / End (then Ctrl+C copies it). On the command line a selection works as in an editor: Left / Right go to its start / end, Backspace / Delete remove it, typing or pasting replaces it, and Ctrl+X cuts it (the command line is found after a prompt ending in $, #, > or %). Full-screen programs such as vim or top still get the keys unchanged.

• Alerts no longer spam. A problem is reported once while it goes on, with a reminder every two hours, instead of again every few minutes for each kind of trouble: a restart loop that also makes the container unhealthy is one alert, and a Swarm service whose tasks all fail (for example an image that doesn't exist) is one alert, not one per replica. Alerts arriving together are one message, desktop notifications come at most every 30 seconds, and the message has Mute 1 h and Pause all 15 min. See Alerts.
  • Cancel switch on a slow server: pressed after Pierside had already connected (an overloaded server answers slowly, so the switch can finish while you reach for the button), it used to do nothing, and you then waited for the slow server to load. Now it takes you back to the engine you came from. Leaving a slow server is also quicker: Pierside waits at most 10 seconds to clean up there.

• Rancher Desktop 1.25: the extension lost its own look (very large headings, uppercase buttons, default colours) because Rancher now provides a minimal theme of its own. Pierside uses its own theme again.

• Root terminal (SSH engines): a switch in the terminal's header opens that server's terminal as root, through a privileged helper container. Off by default, remembered per server, and it asks before turning on. See Remote engines.
  • A file or process action on a server (upload, delete, change permissions, save, end a process) could finish on the other server if you switched engines while it ran. It now stops with a message instead, also when a second window still shows the previous server.
  • Cancel switch stops the switch you see, not whichever one happens to be connecting, and only one switch runs at a time in a window.
  • A server setting (Root terminal, or using Docker where you have no permission) is refused if the active engine changed while you were answering, instead of landing on another server.
  • Containers: the icons of containers inside a Compose project are no longer cut off after a column has been resized.

• Server performance no longer scrolls sideways in a narrow window: the process list leaves out the Running, User, Disk and Container columns as it gets narrower (the command's tooltip shows what they would), and the charts and the switches at the top fit the width.

• Switching away from an SSH engine whose server had been turned off could take minutes, and other engines seemed impossible to switch to meanwhile. Requests waiting for the lost server now get its answer together instead of each trying to reconnect in turn, and the switch no longer waits for clean-up on a server it can't reach.
  • A switch to an engine that doesn't answer can be cancelled: Cancel switch in the engine menu, or Cancel in place of Switch on Manage engines and Engines at a glance.
  • Server performance: on a narrow window, the "Order held" note no longer moves the process list down when it appears, which ended the hold at once.

• Server performance (SSH engines, in the bottom bar): like htop for the server, with the container of each process. CPU, memory, disks and network with 10-minute charts, a note when something stands out (low memory, swapping, waiting for the disk, high load), and the processes sorted by CPU, memory or disk I/O, or grouped by container. Processes can be ended, forced to end or given a lower priority. Nothing has to be installed on the server.
  • Server alerts: switch on Alert me about this server to be told when an SSH server's memory is almost full, it keeps swapping, its load stays high, or a disk is almost full, checked every 30 seconds whichever engine is active.
  • Security: a request to Pierside's local port that claimed to come from a development web page (Origin: http://localhost:3000) was let in without the session token, so any program on your computer, or a web page served on that port, could get full access to Docker through it. Every request now needs the token.
  • Security: AI access accepted names such as ../containers/x for images and networks, which reached other parts of the Docker API: an assistant could delete a container outside its scope or put a container on the host's network. Such names are refused now.
  • Fixed: AI access could start a container on the host's network when given that network's ID instead of its name.
  • Fixed: switching off Watch in the background (or removing a watched engine) left its connection open and could stop the page from updating.
  • Fixed: an unreachable engine could make healthy watched engines look unreachable too.
  • AI access: environment values with spaces were only partly hidden in container_run_command, and compose_config / read_compose_files showed secrets; with "Show environment values" off, variables are no longer filled in, values in environment, build arguments, driver options, inline contents and x- blocks are hidden, and read_compose_files shows the merged configuration instead of the raw files. A volume used by containers outside a connection's scope is no longer visible to it, and lists name only the containers it shares. Starting a container with a host folder mounted now counts as destructive for "ask before destructive actions".
  • Fixed: Swarm "task keeps failing" alerts never came on servers whose clock isn't set to UTC.
  • Fixed: Engines at a glance showed 0 CPU / memory for engines with many containers (now what could be measured, marked "≥"), counted Kubernetes' and Pierside's own containers on the active engine, and could call a container "restarting" hours after it stopped.
  • Fixed: switching engines removed Pierside's helper containers on the new engine instead of the old one, and left shells of the old engine running.
  • Fixed: pruning volumes stopped running file downloads, Server files and disk measurements and debug shells.
  • Fixed: after a brief connection drop (e.g. an SSH hiccup), logs repeated up to 1000 lines; a single failed check could mark a container "removed". Merged Compose logs now also start in time order across slow and fast services.
  • Fixed: Images → Clean up → All unused also deleted the images of Rancher Desktop, Kubernetes and extensions without a running container.
  • Fixed: Swarm stack delete reported success when nothing could be deleted; Compose Start all also started docker compose run one-off containers; Copy docker run command wrote an invalid -p 127.0.0.1:80 for ports with any host port and quoted a multi-word entrypoint as one word.
  • Fixed: a settings file that couldn't be read (engines, port forwards) was overwritten empty on the next change; it is now kept as a copy.
  • Fixed: a second confirmation (e.g. two port conflicts when starting several containers) replaced the first, and the action then never finished.
  • Fixed: in a file browser, a file that loaded slowly could show up, and be saved, under the name of the file clicked after it.
  • Fixed: pausing a container ended its Exec shell and dropped unsaved changes in its Files tab; both now carry on after Resume.
  • Fixed: logs of a container with a terminal (TTY) could clear or switch the log view's screen; only colours and links are kept from such codes now.
  • Fixed: removing an AI connection that was set up "for this project folder only" left it registered in the assistant (for connections set up from now on).
  • Fixed: closing the bottom Docker console left commands such as logs -f running; Ctrl+F no longer takes the key from a shell (vim, less); Images: deleting from an image's page warns about Rancher Desktop's images and removes only the tag shown; IPv6 port links; Swarm secrets and configs show load errors instead of spinning; cancelling a Compose run right after starting it works; lists catch up after the live connection was briefly lost.

• Engines at a glance is its own page now, opened from the second line of the engine switcher at the top of the sidebar. It keeps itself up to date (every 30 seconds by default; 10 seconds to 5 minutes, or only on Refresh), shows the CPU and memory each engine's containers use, and a click on a problem opens the container on its engine.
  • Watch an engine in the background: a switch on each engine's card. A watched engine's alerts (restart loops, out of memory, unhealthy, failing Swarm services) arrive while another engine is active, named with the engine, and you are told when it can't be reached and when it is back. Recent alerts from all engines are listed on the page.
  • Command palette in the Exec tab: save the commands you type often under your own labels and run them in any container's shell with Commands or Ctrl+Shift+P. Each command either runs right away or is only typed so you can change it first, and can be offered everywhere, for an image (postgres, mycorp/*) or for a Compose project / service. One list for all engines, in Rancher and in the separate window.
  • Fixed: with a search in the logs, every batch of new lines moved to the next match and scrolled there. The current match and the view now stay where they are; new matches are still highlighted.
  • Fixed: containers started again and again by something other than Docker, such as a GitLab Runner's job containers, were reported as "keeps restarting" / "keeps crashing". Only containers that Docker itself restarts (restart policy always, unless-stopped, or on-failure after a failure) are reported now.
  • Fixed: on smaller screens, a tooltip near the right edge (such as Refresh on the Server disk page) could make the whole page jump a little to the left.

• Fixed: desktop notifications never appeared inside Rancher Desktop on Windows. They are now shown through Rancher Desktop's own notification call there; the separate window keeps using the browser's.

• Alerts: restart loops are found more reliably. A container whose command keeps finishing cleanly and being restarted is now reported too (with different advice than a crashing one), stopping and starting a container by hand is no longer mistaken for a crash, and slow loops (Docker waits up to a minute between attempts) are no longer missed. New: a Swarm service whose task keeps failing is reported, on any node. See docs/alerts.md.
  • Desktop notifications for these alerts when Pierside is open but not in front; switch them on in the dialog behind the version number.
  • Engines: At a glance. The Engines page shows for every engine whether it can be reached, how many containers run and which need attention, without switching to it.
  • Server disk: the usual places. A list of where space usually goes on a server (Docker's data, container logs, the journal, package caches, temporary files, home folders), measured with one click.
  • File editor: typing in large files is faster.
  • Fixed: switching to the SSH engine that is already active (for example from a second window) broke its connection until you switched away and back.
  • AI access, security:
  • New containers can no longer reach host system folders through a symbolic link: a host path with a link in it is refused, and so is a path inside a folder that a container the assistant can reach mounts writable. The list of refused system folders now also has /etc, /root, /usr, /boot, /bin, /sbin, /lib and, on Windows, Rancher Desktop's WSL socket folder.
  • Answering an assistant's request for more access applies only to the request you saw: if the assistant changed its request meanwhile, nothing is granted and the new request is shown.
  • Engine events no longer show Swarm service, secret and config names to a connection without the Swarm permission.
  • prune of all unused images keeps the images of Rancher Desktop extensions and Kubernetes, as it promised.
  • Asking for a wider file path or name pattern than a connection has (e.g. /app/** when it has /app/*) now reaches you instead of being answered "already allowed".
  • Adding an SSH engine shows the server's host-key fingerprint first; your password or key is sent only after you confirm it.
  • Downloads from volumes, containers and server files fail visibly if they are cut short, instead of saving a shorter file; long downloads and uploads through Pierside's helper containers are no longer interrupted after a minute.
  • Logs: lines are no longer dropped when a container writes to stdout and stderr at the same moment.
  • Live views (logs, shell, stats, pull progress, terminal) reconnect by themselves after Pierside's backend restarts, instead of staying disconnected until Pierside is reopened.
  • Port forwards to SSH engines follow a container that was recreated (new address or port), and go away when it is removed, instead of reaching whatever now has its old address.
  • Server files: uploading into, or downloading from, a place your SSH user can't access asks whether Docker may be used, instead of showing "[object Object]".
  • Containers: "Remove service" on a Swarm service asks first and reports the result.
  • Cancelling docker compose on an SSH engine stops it on the server; stopping Server disk stops its measurements there too.

Pierside 1.0: next to Docker itself, it now also works with the server behind an SSH engine.

  • Server files: with an SSH engine active, Server files in the bottom bar browses and edits the files of that server with the same file browser and editor, as your SSH user. Where that user has no permission but may use Docker, Pierside can work through a short-lived helper container instead (asked once per server, marked with a badge, read-only unless you change something).
  • Server disk: next to it, Server disk shows how full the server's filesystems are and which folders take the space. Folders are measured one by one as you open them, at low priority, with a time limit and a stop button; folders you can't read can be measured through Docker. It only reads.
  • Find by name in every file browser (containers, volumes, server files): typing narrows the current folder, Enter searches its subfolders.
  • File editor:
  • Review changes shows your edit as a diff before saving.
  • Syntax errors in JSON and YAML are underlined, and Compose files are checked against the official Compose schema (bundled, nothing is downloaded).
  • VS Code keyboard shortcuts (Ctrl+D, Alt+Up/Down, Ctrl+/, Ctrl+L and more).
  • Bracket pair colours and indentation guides.
  • AI access:
  • Add to Claude Code / Add to Devin CLI registers a connection with one click, for all your projects or for one project folder you choose, through a small helper program Rancher Desktop installs with the extension. The dialog shows the command the button runs. Removing a connection also removes it from the assistant.
  • The connection dialog is simpler, and says when a connection is trusted instead of promising a question that won't come.
  • Containers: a Compose project that is partly running has a start button for its stopped containers next to Stop all, in the list and on the project page.
  • Files in containers: a folder the container's user can't read now says "Permission denied" instead of looking empty.
  • Docs: What works where lists what differs between the Pierside tab in Rancher Desktop and the separate window, and between the local engine and SSH engines, with the reason for each.
• AI access: the connection dialog also shows the command for Devin CLI (devin mcp add).

• AI access: a built-in MCP server for assistants such as Claude Code, with 66 tools covering containers, files, Compose projects, images, volumes, networks, ports, engine information, clean-up and Swarm, on the local engine and on SSH engines. Each connection has its own limits: which engines and containers, which of 20 permissions, and which file paths; or "Allow everything". By default no secret is stored with the assistant: you allow each session in Pierside, or trust a connection for a period or for good, actions that change something can ask every time, and the assistant can ask you for more access when it needs it; an access token is available for unattended use. Calls are listed under Recent activity. See docs/ai-access.md.
  • Troubleshooting: what to do when installing reports invalid extension metadata.

First release under the name Pierside.

  • Containers: live list grouped by Compose project; start, stop, restart and delete for single containers, projects and selections; port links; port-conflict hints; health checks; alerts for containers that crash, restart in a loop or run out of memory.
  • Container details: logs (search, timestamps, download, copy as Markdown), inspect, bind mounts, interactive shell, debug shell for containers without one, file browser, live stats.
  • Compose: merged colour-coded logs; Up, Down, Pull and recreate and View configuration with the common flags; projects stay listed after down.
  • Files: upload, edit in a code editor with syntax highlighting, delete and change permissions, in containers and volumes.
  • Images: pull, run with options, layers, prune, copy to another engine.
  • Volumes and networks: create, inspect and prune; connect and disconnect containers. Items that belong to Rancher Desktop extensions are hidden unless you show them, are skipped by Prune, and deleting one asks with a warning first.
  • Disk usage: what takes space, with one-click cleanup.
  • Ports: forward container ports to localhost, also from remote servers.
  • Remote engines over SSH, each with its own name and colour.
  • Swarm: stacks, services, tasks, nodes, secrets and configs.
  • Terminal: Docker console locally, a full shell on SSH engines.
  • Updates: the footer shows the version and tells you when a newer release exists; old Pierside images are removed automatically.

docs.title: Compose projects
docs.text: Containers started by Docker Compose are grouped into a project row on the Containers page. The row shows how many services are running and has project-wide Start, Stop, Restart and Delete.

docs.title: Project view
docs.text:
Click a project to open it:

  • Logs of all services merged into one stream, ordered by time, each line prefixed with the service name in its own colour. Hide or show services, search, toggle timestamps, download.
  • Services with their status and actions; click one for the container's details.

docs.title: Up, Down and friends
docs.text:
Pierside remembers where each project's Compose files are, separately for each engine, so a project stays listed after docker compose down and can be brought up again. The ⋮ menu of a project has:

  • Up and Down: a dialog with the common options (--build, --pull always, --force-recreate, --remove-orphans, selected services with --no-deps, profiles, env file, extra arguments). It shows the exact command and streams its output. Up always runs detached (up -d).
  • Pull and recreate: pulls newer images and recreates the containers that use them.
  • View configuration: the resolved Compose file (docker compose config).

The options you used last are remembered per project. The ▶ button on a stopped project runs Up with them.

Open compose file on the Containers page adds a project that has never been started.

docs.title: Where the command runs
docs.text:
• Local engine: Pierside runs the real docker compose on your machine through Rancher Desktop, so builds, relative paths and .env files behave as in a terminal. This works in the Pierside tab inside Rancher Desktop. It is not available in the separate browser window, because only Rancher Desktop may run commands on your machine.
  • SSH engine: the command runs on the server, where the files are. The server needs the docker compose plugin. This also works in the separate window.

See What works where for the other differences between the two views and the two kinds of engine.

docs.title: If something fails
docs.text: The dialog shows Compose's own output and explains the usual causes: the Compose file was moved or deleted, the Compose plugin is missing, or a port is already in use.

docs.title: Container files
docs.text:
A running container's Files tab is a file browser for its filesystem:

  • navigate, preview and download files;
  • upload with the button or by dropping files on the list;
  • create files and folders, delete them;
  • edit text files up to 1 MB;
  • change permissions by clicking a value in the Mode column (a read/write/execute grid or an octal number; for folders optionally everything inside).

Edits keep the file's owner and permissions. New files belong to the container's user.

These actions use tools inside the container (ls, rm, chmod), so they need a container that has them. For minimal images without a shell, use the debug shell in the Exec tab.

docs.title: Volume contents
docs.text: A volume's Stored data tab is the same browser for the volume. Pierside reads the volume through a short-lived helper container that mounts it read-only. Only when you change something does it start a second helper that mounts the volume writable. Both are removed afterwards. New files get the owner of the folder they are created in.

docs.title: Find a file by name
docs.text:
Every file browser (container files, volume contents, Server files) has a Find by name box in its path bar.

  • Typing narrows the folder you are in at once.
  • Enter also looks through its subfolders and lists the matches with where they are. Click a file to open it, or a folder to go there. The cross in the box brings the folder back.

Upper and lower case don't matter, and the text is taken literally (* is just a star). A search returns at most 500 matches and is stopped after 20 seconds on a very large tree; it then says so, and searching from a subfolder gets the rest. It never looks into /proc, /sys or /dev, and doesn't follow symbolic links. On Server files it runs with your own rights and says when folders you can't read were skipped; with Docker allowed for that server it searches those too.

docs.title: Files on the server (SSH engines)
docs.text:
With an SSH engine active, Server files in the bottom bar, next to Terminal, browses and edits the files of that server itself, with the same browser and editor. It starts in your home folder; the pin button next to the path takes you to any folder by typing its path.

Everything runs as your SSH user, with that user's rights. A folder you can read lists all its entries, including files you can't open, with their owner and permissions.

Where you have no permission. If your SSH user may use Docker on the server (it is in the docker group, for example), Pierside can do the same through a short-lived helper container that mounts the folder, as root. The first time you hit such a file or folder, Pierside asks whether to do that on this server and remembers the answer; the switch Use Docker where I have no permission at the top of the page changes it later. While a file is handled this way, the path bar shows Through Docker (root); otherwise it shows As and your user name.

  • Reading and browsing use a read-only mount; only saving, uploading, creating, deleting and changing permissions use a separate writable one. The helpers are removed after a minute without use.
  • A file you save keeps its owner and permissions. A new file or folder gets the owner of the folder it is created in.
  • Not mounted: the root folder itself (files directly in / are only reachable with your own rights) and /proc, /sys, /dev.
  • Docker can't help when it runs rootless or with user-namespace remapping on the server, as its containers then have no more rights than you; the switch says so.
  • On servers with SELinux enforcing, a mount may still be refused. Pierside doesn't relabel files to get around that.

Being allowed to use Docker on a server is as good as being root there, and this makes it one click away. Check that working this way is fine where you work.

docs.title: Disk space on the server (SSH engines)
docs.text:
Server disk in the bottom bar shows where the space on the server went. It only reads; nothing can be deleted from it.

  • At the top are the server's filesystems with how full they are. This is immediate.
  • Below them, The usual places lists where space usually goes on a server: Docker's data, container logs, the systemd journal, package caches, temporary files, home folders, limited to what exists on this server. Measure these measures them one after another; some come with a hint on how to shrink them. Click one to open it.
  • Click one to open it. Pierside lists the folder and then measures each subfolder, so the rows fill in one after another, largest first, each with a bar and its share. Click a folder to go deeper; the folder button at the right opens the same place in Server files.
  • Nothing is measured that you didn't open, and sizes you have seen are kept while the page is open, so going back up is instant. Refresh measures the current folder again.

Measuring a folder with a great many files takes time on any system. It runs at the lowest CPU and disk priority, so the server's own work comes first, at most two folders at a time, and a single folder is given two minutes; one that takes longer is marked, and opening it measures its parts one by one. The stop button ends what is running. Sizes count each folder's own filesystem only, so a disk mounted inside it is not added.

Folders your SSH user can't read fully are marked Partly unreadable, because their real size is larger. If your account may use Docker on the server, Pierside offers to measure those through a read-only helper container, as root; this is the same choice as for Server files, is remembered per server, and can be changed with the switch Use Docker where I have no permission at the top of either page. Such rows show Through Docker. The root folder itself and /proc, /sys, /dev are never mounted.

Docker's own data (images, volumes, build cache) is broken down on the Disk usage page.

docs.title: The editor
docs.text:
Files open in a code editor, first as a read-only preview:

  • syntax highlighting chosen from the file name (YAML, JSON, Dockerfile, nginx, shell, INI, TOML, Python, JavaScript/TypeScript, SQL, HTML/CSS/XML, Markdown, Go, Rust and more). The language button next to the file name picks another.
  • line numbers, folding, search and replace (Ctrl+F), multiple cursors, undo.
  • Edit unlocks the view; Ctrl+S saves.
  • Review changes (the button next to Save) shows your edit as a diff against the file as it was loaded: removed lines in red above the new ones in green, long unchanged stretches folded. Save from there, or click the button again to go back to editing. A change of line endings is mentioned above the diff.
  • LF/CRLF sets the line endings written to disk. Files that mix both are flagged.
  • Error checking for JSON and YAML: syntax errors are underlined in red with a marker in the gutter; hover for the message. Compose files (compose.yaml, docker-compose.yml, compose.override.yaml, docker-compose.prod.yml and so on) are also checked against the official Compose schema, which is built into Pierside (nothing is downloaded); schema problems are underlined in yellow on the key or value concerned. YAML files over 200 KB aren't checked, and Compose files over 100 KB get the syntax check only. Picking JSON or YAML with the language button checks the file as that language.
  • Keyboard shortcuts as in VS Code: Ctrl+D select the next occurrence, Alt+Up/Down move lines, Shift+Alt+Up/Down copy lines, Ctrl+/ toggle comment, Ctrl+Shift+K delete line, Ctrl+L select line (again for the next one), Ctrl+Enter / Ctrl+Shift+Enter insert a line below / above, Tab / Shift+Tab indent / unindent the selection.
  • Matching brackets are coloured by nesting depth, and indentation guides show the structure of nested blocks.
  • Wrap lines toggles wrapping; Maximize expands the editor over the whole window (Esc restores); drag the divider to resize.

docs.title: Logs as Markdown
docs.text: Select lines in any log view and choose Copy as Markdown to get a ready-to-paste block with the source, the time range and full timestamps.

docs.title: Copy an image to another engine
docs.text: From an image's ⋮ menu or detail page you can copy the image to another engine, for example from your laptop to an SSH server. It is streamed directly; no registry is involved.

docs.title: Before you install
docs.text:
1. Install Rancher Desktop 1.23 or newer.
  2. In Rancher Desktop, open Preferences → Container Engine and choose dockerd (moby). Pierside talks to the Docker socket; with containerd it shows a message asking you to switch.

rdctl and docker come with Rancher Desktop. If your terminal doesn't find them, open a new terminal after Rancher Desktop has started.

docs.title: Install
docs.text:
rdctl extension install ghcr.io/hemi131/pierside:latest

Open Pierside in Rancher Desktop's sidebar. Images are published for amd64 and arm64.

docs.title: Which tag?
docs.text: Tag What you get latest The newest release. 0.1.0, 0.2.0, … Exactly that release. It never changes. edge The current development build. It can be broken; use it only to try something unreleased.

docs.title: Update
docs.text:
When a newer release exists, Pierside's footer shows Update available. Click it for the commands that match your installation.

If you installed latest:

docker pull ghcr.io/hemi131/pierside:latest
rdctl extension uninstall ghcr.io/hemi131/pierside:latest
rdctl extension install ghcr.io/hemi131/pierside:latest

If you installed a version number, replace the old number with the new one:

rdctl extension uninstall ghcr.io/hemi131/pierside:0.1.0
rdctl extension install ghcr.io/hemi131/pierside:0.2.0

docs.title: Why install alone doesn't update
docs.text:
Rancher Desktop has two behaviours that surprise people:

  • Installing a tag that is already installed does nothing, even though it prints Created.
  • It never downloads a newer image for a tag you already have locally. After an uninstall, install …:latest reuses the old latest stored on your machine.

So latest needs a docker pull first, and any update needs an uninstall. Version numbers avoid the second problem, because a new number has never been on your machine.

docs.title: Which version am I running?
docs.text: The footer shows it (for example Pierside 0.2.0). Click it for the About dialog.

docs.title: What survives an update
docs.text: Engines, SSH keys, remembered Compose projects, port forwards and the update-check setting live in a Docker volume named pierside-data, which uninstalling does not remove. View settings such as column widths are stored by Rancher Desktop with the extension and normally survive as well.

docs.title: Old images
docs.text: Rancher Desktop does not delete an extension's previous image. Each time Pierside starts, it removes old Pierside images that no container uses: untagged ones, and older version numbers of the copy you installed. It never touches other images.

docs.title: Update check
docs.text: Once a day Pierside asks GitHub for the newest release number of this repository. Nothing about your installation is sent. To switch it off, click the version in the footer and turn off Check for new versions.

docs.title: Uninstall
docs.text:
rdctl extension uninstall ghcr.io/hemi131/pierside:latest

To also delete Pierside's saved data (engines, SSH keys, settings):

docker volume ls --filter name=pierside-data
docker volume rm <the volume name shown>

docs.title: Ports and forwarding
docs.text:
The Ports page lists three things:

  • ports Pierside is forwarding,
  • ports that containers publish,
  • ports that containers expose but nobody publishes.

docs.title: Forward a port
docs.text:
Forward a port (on the Ports page, or in a container's ⋮ menu) makes a container port reachable at localhost:<port> on your computer without recreating the container.

  • Local engine: useful for a container that was started without -p.
  • SSH engine: brings a remote container's port to your computer through Pierside's SSH connection, even when the port isn't published on the server. Nothing is opened on the server.

Each forward is a small helper container on your local engine. Forwards survive switching engines and restarting Pierside, disappear when their target container is removed, and are removed when Pierside is uninstalled.

docs.title: Port conflicts
docs.text: Starting a container whose host port is already taken shows which container holds the port and offers to stop it.

docs.title: This website
docs.text:
This website doesn't use cookies, analytics, advertising or any other tracking, and it doesn't load fonts or scripts from other sites.

  • Hosting. The site is served by GitHub Pages. Like any web server, GitHub receives your IP address and the usual request details (the page, your browser) and may keep them in its logs, for example for security. The GitHub General Privacy Statement applies to that.
  • Repository details in the header. To show the latest version and the number of stars of the GitHub repository, your browser asks GitHub's public API (api.github.com) for them once per visit and keeps the answer for the rest of the visit in its session storage.
  • Your colour scheme (light, dark or automatic) is remembered in your browser's local storage. It never leaves your browser.
  • Search runs entirely in your browser.
  • Links to GitHub, Docker Hub and other sites lead to services with their own privacy policies.

docs.title: The Pierside extension
docs.text: Pierside runs entirely on your machine. An AI assistant only sees what you share with it under AI access, which is off until you create a connection. The only request Pierside makes on its own is a once-a-day check of the newest release number on GitHub, which sends nothing about your installation and can be switched off (click the version in Pierside's footer).

docs.title: Questions
docs.text: Pierside is an independent open-source project. Questions about this page are welcome as GitHub issues.

docs.text: Pierside is not affiliated with, endorsed or sponsored by Docker, Inc., SUSE, Anthropic, Cognition or GitHub. Docker, Docker Desktop, Docker Hub, Rancher, Rancher Desktop, Claude, Claude Code, Devin, GitHub and other names mentioned on this site are trademarks of their respective owners and are used only to describe compatibility.

docs.title: Remote engines over SSH
docs.text: Pierside can manage Docker on another machine through SSH. Nothing is installed on the server.

docs.title: Add an engine
docs.text:
1. Open the engine switcher at the top of the sidebar and choose Engines → Add SSH engine.
  2. Enter the host, the user, and a private key (paste it) or a password.
  3. Check host key shows the server's host-key fingerprint before anything is sent to the server. Compare it with the server's own (ssh-keygen -lf /etc/ssh/ssh_host_ed25519_key.pub on the server) and confirm it.
  4. Test connection then logs in, only to a server with that key, and checks Docker. Save when it works.

Switch engines from the same menu. Everything in Pierside (containers, images, volumes, logs, shell, files) then works on the selected engine.

docs.title: What the server needs
docs.text:
• An SSH server you can log in to.
  • Docker, and a user that may use the Docker socket: a member of the docker group, or rootless Docker.
  • For Compose actions: the docker compose plugin on the server.

Pierside reaches the Docker socket by SSH socket forwarding. If the server disallows forwarding, it falls back to docker system dial-stdio automatically.

docs.title: Colours
docs.text: Give an engine a colour (when adding it, or Engines → Colour). While that engine is active, Pierside is framed in the colour and shows a banner with the engine's name. A red frame for production makes it hard to delete the wrong thing.

docs.title: Engines at a glance
docs.text:
Engines at a glance, the second line of the engine switcher at the top of the sidebar, has a card for every engine, without switching to it:

  • whether it can be reached, and how many containers run;
  • the CPU and memory its running containers use (100% is one core);
  • which containers need attention: restarting, unhealthy, dead, or exited with an error in the last hours. Hover a problem to see the containers' names; click it to switch to that engine and open the (first) container's logs.

The page keeps itself up to date while it is open: every 30 seconds by default, or every 10 seconds, minute or 5 minutes, or only when you press Refresh (the menu at the top right). Switch makes an engine the active one.

docs.title: Watching an engine in the background
docs.text:
Switch on Watch in the background on an engine's card to keep an eye on it while you work on another engine:

  • its card stays up to date even while the page is closed;
  • its alerts (restart loops, out of memory, unhealthy, failing Swarm services) are shown like the active engine's, with the engine's name;
  • you are told when it can't be reached, and again when it is back.

Pierside keeps a connection to each watched engine open for this. The alerts of every engine are listed under Recent alerts on the page, also those that came while no Pierside window was open (until Rancher Desktop is restarted).

docs.title: Server performance
docs.text:
Server performance in the bottom bar is like htop for the server, with each process's container next to it. Nothing has to be installed on the server: Pierside reads the figures over the SSH connection every 2 seconds while the page is open, and stops when you leave it.

  • At the top: CPU (with the time spent waiting for the disk, and "steal" on a virtual machine whose host is overloaded), memory (with the cache the system gives back when needed, and swap), disks and network, with charts of the last 10 minutes.
  • A note when something stands out: memory almost full, the server swapping, the CPU waiting for the disk, high load.
  • Processes: CPU, memory, disk reads and writes, how long they have been running, and the command. Click a column to sort, search by command, user, container or process number, or Group by container to see at once how much each container uses, and how much the server's own processes do. 100 % CPU is one full core, as in htop. While the pointer is on the list, its rows stay in place (the figures keep updating), so a row and its ⋮ don't move away under the pointer; new processes are added at the bottom and ended ones are greyed out. Hold order under the pointer (on by default) switches this off.
  • What you can do with a process (the ⋮ menu): open its container, copy its command line, Lower priority, End (asks it to stop) or Force end (stops it at once). Each asks first and shows exactly which process (its name and user as the system knows them, and its command line), with a warning for processes the server depends on, such as sshd or dockerd. A container's main process ignores End; use Force end, or stop the container.

As your SSH user, Pierside sees every process's CPU and memory, but disk reads and writes only for your own processes, and you can only end your own. With Use Docker where I have no permission switched on (at the top of the page; the same setting as in Server files and Server disk), everything is read and done as root, through a short-lived helper container on the server that is removed when you leave the page. It shares the server's processes (not its files or network) and may read every process's I/O figures and change its priority.

Alert me about this server (at the top of the page) checks the server every 30 seconds, also while you work on another engine: you get an alert when its memory is almost full, it keeps swapping, its load stays high, or a disk is 90 % full.

docs.title: What differs on a remote engine
docs.text:
Most of Pierside works the same on a remote engine. In short:

  • Compose runs on the server, where the project's files are, instead of on your computer.
  • Terminal in the bottom bar is a full shell on the server instead of a Docker console. With its Root terminal switch on, it opens as root on that server (see below).
  • Server files, Server performance and Server disk in the bottom bar show the server itself: its files, what uses its CPU, memory, disks and network, and what takes its disk space. They exist only for SSH engines.
  • Port links open the server's address, and Forward a port brings a remote container's port to your localhost through the SSH connection.

The full list, with the reason for each difference, is in What works where.

docs.title: Root terminal
docs.text:
The Root terminal switch in the terminal's header opens that server's terminal as root, without a password. It is off by default, remembered per server, and asks before it turns on. A red root mark shows while a session really is root.

  • How it works: Pierside starts a privileged helper container on the server, and the shell enters the server's own namespaces. It is a shell on the server, not in a container. Anyone who may use Docker on a server can already become root there; this makes it one switch.
  • Not recorded by sudo: it bypasses the server's sudo rules and sudo log. Use it only if you are allowed to be root on that server.
  • When the terminal closes or loses its connection (network drop, computer asleep, switching engines), the helper is removed and everything started in the session ends, including tmux, screen and nohup jobs. A system upgrade or a migration could be left half done, so start long jobs through the server's service manager (systemd-run, systemctl start), which keeps them running.
  • It needs no SSH terminal, so it can work where the SSH account isn't allowed one. It does need a privileged container and the alpine helper image.
  • When it isn't possible (rootless Docker, user namespace remapping, or privileged containers refused), the terminal says why and opens your normal shell, without the root mark.
  • AI assistants can't use it.

docs.title: Where credentials are stored
docs.text:
Keys and passwords are stored in Pierside's data volume (pierside-data) on your machine and are only used to open the SSH connection. Removing an engine deletes its stored key. Anyone who can use Docker on your machine can read that volume, as they can read any volume.

They are stored as they are needed to connect: a password in plain text, a key together with its passphrase. A passphrase therefore doesn't protect the key while it is stored there; nothing inside Rancher Desktop's VM could keep it better. Give Pierside a key of its own (for example ssh-keygen -t ed25519 -f ~/.ssh/pierside, added to the server's authorized_keys) rather than your personal one, so you can revoke it on its own.

docs.title: "Engine unavailable" or a message about the container engine
docs.text: Pierside needs the dockerd (moby) engine. Check Preferences → Container Engine in Rancher Desktop, and that Rancher Desktop has finished starting.

docs.title: The footer says "Polling"
docs.text: Live updates use a WebSocket to Pierside's backend on a localhost port. If that connection can't be made, Pierside refreshes every 3 seconds instead; logs, shell and stats may not work. This can happen right after installing while Rancher Desktop is still starting. Restart Rancher Desktop, or uninstall and install Pierside again.

docs.title: Installing didn't give me the new version
docs.text: Rancher Desktop reuses the image already on your machine. Follow Update: docker pull, uninstall, install.

docs.title: invalid extension metadata / 422 Unprocessable Entity when installing
docs.text:
Rancher Desktop could not download the image, usually because of a network or DNS problem, and reports it this way. Download it yourself to see the real error, then install:

docker pull ghcr.io/hemi131/pierside:latest
rdctl extension install ghcr.io/hemi131/pierside:latest

If docker pull fails with a timeout, try again in a moment or check your network, VPN or DNS.

docs.title: A container has no shell
docs.text: Minimal images have no sh. The Exec tab offers a debug shell: a helper container that shares the container's processes and network and starts in its filesystem. It is removed when you close the session.

docs.title: Compose actions are greyed out
docs.text: On the local engine, Compose commands run through Rancher Desktop and are only available in the Pierside tab inside Rancher Desktop, not in the separate browser window. See Compose projects and What works where.

docs.title: unknown flag: --ansi when running Compose on a server
docs.text: The server has no docker compose plugin. Install it on the server.

docs.title: Swarm services aren't reachable on their published port
docs.text: Rancher Desktop doesn't support Swarm's ingress routing mesh. Publish ports with mode: host. Pierside flags ingress ports.

docs.title: Backend logs
docs.text:
docker ps --filter label=com.pierside.backend=true
docker logs <container id>

Include these when you report a problem.

docs.title: What works where
docs.text: Most of Pierside works the same everywhere. A few features depend on two things: whether you use Pierside inside Rancher Desktop or in its separate window, and whether the active engine is the local one or a server over SSH. This page lists those differences and the reason for each.

docs.title: Inside Rancher Desktop or in the separate window
docs.text:
Pierside normally runs as a tab inside Rancher Desktop. Open in separate window, at the bottom of the sidebar, opens the same Pierside in your web browser, which is handy on a second monitor.

The difference comes from one rule: only Rancher Desktop may start programs on your computer. A page in a web browser can't, and Pierside doesn't try to get around that. Everything that only talks to Docker works in both.

Feature Inside Rancher Desktop Separate window Why Containers, images, volumes, networks, ports, disk usage, Swarm, logs, shells in containers, files Yes Yes Pierside's backend does this through the Docker engine. Compose Up, Down, Pull, View configuration on the local engine Yes No Pierside runs the real docker compose on your computer, which only Rancher Desktop can start. The same Compose commands on an SSH engine Yes Yes They run on the server, over Pierside's SSH connection. Open compose file on the local engine Yes No It uses Rancher Desktop's file dialog and then runs Compose on your computer. Terminal: Docker console (local engine) Yes No It runs docker commands on your computer through Rancher Desktop. Terminal: shell on the server (SSH engine) Yes Yes It goes over the SSH connection. AI access: Add to Claude Code / Devin CLI and the folder chooser Yes No The button runs the assistant's own command on your computer. In the separate window, copy the command and run it yourself. AI access: everything else (connections, approvals, activity) Yes Yes Server files and Server disk (SSH engine) Yes Yes Alerts and desktop notifications Yes Yes In Rancher Desktop the notification is Rancher's own (fixed title, no click action); in the separate window it is the browser's, which asks for permission once.

Other things to know about the separate window:

  • It is opened from Rancher Desktop. The link works once and only on your computer. After Pierside restarts (an update, or Rancher Desktop restarting), the window says its session has expired; open it again from the sidebar.
  • View settings are kept separately. Column widths, filters, the collapsed sidebar and similar settings are remembered per view, so changing them in the window doesn't change them in Rancher Desktop. Engines, AI access connections and everything else Pierside stores are shared.
  • Approval questions appear in both. A question from an AI assistant shows up wherever Pierside is open; answering it in one place closes it in the other.

docs.title: Local engine or SSH engine
docs.text:
The local engine is the Docker inside Rancher Desktop on your computer. An SSH engine is Docker on another machine, which Pierside reaches through an SSH connection (see Remote engines over SSH). Lists, logs, shells, stats, files in containers and volumes, images, networks and Swarm work the same on both. These differ:

Feature Local engine SSH engine Why Compose Up, Down, Pull, View configuration Runs docker compose on your computer, through Rancher Desktop (not in the separate window) Runs docker compose on the server Compose needs the project's files, so it runs where they are. The server needs the docker compose plugin. Open compose file A file dialog on your computer You type the file's path on the server Same reason: the file is on the server. Terminal in the bottom bar Docker console: docker … commands only A full shell on the server, as your SSH user Locally there is no server to log in to; Rancher Desktop runs the Docker commands. Server files Not available Browse and edit the server's own files, with Docker as a fallback where your user has no permission Locally the "server" would be Rancher Desktop's internal Linux VM, and your own files are already on your computer. Server disk Not available See how full the server's filesystems are and which folders take the space Same reason. Docker's own data is on the Disk usage page for both kinds of engine. Port links in the lists Open localhost:<port> Open the server's address (or the Host for port links set for the engine) A published port is published on the machine the engine runs on. Forward a port Makes a container port reachable on localhost without recreating the container The same, for a container on the server, through the SSH connection; nothing is opened on the server Forwards always end on your computer. Host folders when running an image A Windows path such as C:\data is translated for you Paths are paths on the server A mounted folder is always a folder of the machine the engine runs on. Containers of Rancher Desktop itself (Kubernetes, extensions) Hidden unless you show them; protected from Prune Usually none They belong to Rancher Desktop on your computer. AI access: Compose tools (up, down, read files, configuration) Not available; the assistant gets the files' location instead Available An AI connection has no access to Rancher Desktop's window, which is where local Compose runs. On a server Pierside runs Compose itself.

Not a difference, though it is easy to assume one: the AI access permissions (apart from the Compose tools), the protection of Pierside's own containers and copying images between engines behave the same on both kinds of engine.
